title: Veni Sancte Spiritus (Come, Holy Spirit)
text:
Come, Holy Spirit,
and send forth from heaven
the ray of your light.

Come, Father of the poor;
come, giver of gifts;
come, light of hearts.

Best consoler,
sweet guest of the soul,
sweet coolness:

In labor, rest;
in heat, refreshment;
in tears, solace.

O most blessed light,
fill the inmost heart
of your faithful.

Without your divine power,
there is nothing in man,
and nothing innocent.

Cleanse what is base,
water what is dry,
heal what is wounded.

Bend what is rigid,
warm what is chilled,
make right what is crooked.

Give to your faithful,
who trust in you,
the sevenfold gifts.

Grant the reward of virtue,
grant the deliverance of salvation,
grant eternal joy.

Amen.

translation.latin:
Veni, Sancte Spiritus,
et emitte caelitus
lucis tuae radium.

Veni, pater pauperum,
veni, dator munerum,
veni, lumen cordium.

Consolator optime,
dulcis hospes animae,
dulce refrigerium:

In labore requies,
in aestu temperies,
in fletu solatium.

O lux beatissima,
reple cordis intima
tuorum fidelium.

Sine tuo numine,
nihil est in homine,
et nihil innoxium.

Lava quod est sordidum,
riga quod est aridum,
sana quod est saucium.

Flecte quod est rigidum,
fove quod est frigidum,
rege quod est devium.

Da tuis fidelibus,
in te confidentibus,
sacrum septenarium.

Da virtutis meritum,
da salutis exitum,
da perenne gaudium.

Amen.

attribution: Attributed to Stephen Langton (c. 1150-1228), Archbishop of Canterbury
notes:
The Veni Sancte Spiritus, often called the 'Golden Sequence,' is a medieval sequence hymn sung before the Gospel on Pentecost Sunday. It is one of only four sequences preserved in the Roman Missal after the Council of Trent (the others being Victimae Paschali Laudes for Easter, Lauda Sion for Corpus Christi, and Stabat Mater for Our Lady of Sorrows; the Dies Irae was later moved to the Liturgy of the Hours).

Traditionally attributed to Stephen Langton, Archbishop of Canterbury (c. 1150-1228), this hymn is noted for its poetic beauty and deep theology of the Holy Spirit. The sequence invokes the Spirit as consoler, light, and source of the seven gifts (wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord).

The three-fold structure of the hymn (purifying, healing, and perfecting) mirrors the soul's journey toward God, while the recurring refrain 'Veni' (Come) expresses the Church's longing for the Spirit's presence.
description: The Golden Sequence for Pentecost Sunday, a poetic hymn invoking the Holy Spirit with sevenfold gifts
